title: Tennis Levels the Playing Field: Equal Prize Money at Top Events
summary:
For years, women tennis players have fought for something simple: equal pay for equal work. Now, they're getting it at the highest level outside the Grand Slams.

The Women's Tennis Association (WTA) announced that starting next year, all combined 1,000 events — the biggest tournaments where both men and women compete — will award equal prize money. Some, like Indian Wells, Miami, Madrid and Beijing, already did, along with all four Grand Slams. But the Italian Open, Canadian Open and Cincinnati Open will now follow suit. This fulfills a long-standing goal for the WTA, which was founded in 1973 to grow women's tennis. In fact, Italian Open organizers had promised back in 2023 to offer equal prize money by 2025, but they never followed through — until now.

"Achieving equal prize money across all combined WTA 1,000 tournaments is a major milestone for tennis," said WTA chair Valerie Camillo. She added it shows the WTA's commitment to "leading the sports industry in delivering our athletes competitive and financial equality."

The WTA also made changes to the calendar to give players more flexibility. Top-50 players now must play only four WTA 500 events instead of six. They can also swap one WTA 1,000 result for a stronger WTA 500 or 250 result. "We have listened to player feedback on the demands of the calendar," Camillo said.

American world number three Jessica Pegula welcomed the news: "The 2027 changes give us more ability to build our seasons around our own goals — competitively and personally. That's an impactful step forward for players."

It's a win that goes beyond money — it's about respect, fairness, and giving athletes control over their careers.
why_it_matters: Pay in elite sport shapes what millions of young people grow up believing is normal, so teenagers today will enter workplaces where 'equal pay for equal work' is treated as expected rather than something to demand. It also shows how slowly change can come: the fight in tennis has run for over fifty years and is still not finished everywhere.

background_read: The Women's Tennis Association (the WTA — the organization that runs the women's professional tennis tour) was founded in 1973, the same year the American champion Billie Jean King beat Bobby Riggs in a famous 'Battle of the Sexes' match that made the world take women's tennis seriously.

That same year the US Open became the first of the Grand Slams to award equal prize money to men and women; Wimbledon and the French Open did not follow until 2007, after years of campaigning by players such as Venus Williams.
Even now the gap has not closed everywhere: many smaller tournaments still pay women less, and in sports like football and cricket the difference is far bigger.

Jessica Pegula (an American player ranked third in the world) called the WTA's plan an 'impactful step forward', while Valerie Camillo (the WTA chair, who leads the tour's board) said it shows tennis is 'leading the sports industry' on equality.

perspectives.description: Equal prize money at the biggest combined events means women are paid the same as men for the same work, and players like Jessica Pegula say the new calendar rules give them more control over their seasons. The WTA hopes the move strengthens its position with sponsors and broadcasters.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — the change is narrower than it sounds
perspectives.description: It covers only top 'combined 1,000' tournaments, while smaller events, lower-ranked players and most other sports still pay women much less. Critics argue one announcement does not fix deeper gaps in sponsorship, media coverage and coaching.

Tennis has led other sports on pay since the 1970s, but progress has come in slow steps, with decades between the US Open's move and Wimbledon's. Big shifts in sport usually follow organized pressure from players rather than arriving on their own.

The open question is whether football, cricket or basketball follow the model, and whether equal pay filters down to smaller tennis tournaments. The Italian Open's broken 2025 promise shows why players and fans will keep checking that the money actually arrives.
